presenterNotes: Block 1: Emphasize the connection between stem‑and‑leaf plots and histograms. Show how splitting stems gives finer detail. The concept of an outlier is important.
Block 2: Dot plots are intuitive. Use a quick classroom activity: have students create a dot plot of their own text messages or shoe sizes.
Block 3: Pie charts are familiar, but the calculation of central angles is a key skill. Pareto charts are powerful in business contexts — use the inventory shrinkage example to illustrate.
Block 4: Scatter plots preview correlation (Chapter 9). Time series charts are common in media; show examples from news articles.
Block 5: The blueprint flowchart is a handy summary. Encourage students to use it as a reference when they encounter new data.

formulaCard.title: How to Build a Stem‑and‑Leaf Plot

explanation: A [[kw:stem‑and‑leaf plot]] is a graphical display of quantitative data where each number is split into a stem (the leading digit(s)) and a leaf (the final digit).
[[imp:Stems are listed in a column to the left of a vertical line; leaves go to the right.]]
Each leaf corresponds to one data entry, so the number of leaves equals the sample size.
The plot can be [[kw:unordered]] (leaves in original order) or [[kw:ordered]] (leaves sorted from smallest to largest). An ordered plot makes it easy to find the minimum, maximum, and median.
A [[kw:key]] is essential — it shows how to read a stem and leaf combination, e.g., $ 15 | 5 = 155 $.
If data are spread over many stems, you can split each stem into two rows: one for leaves 0–4 and one for leaves 5–9. This gives a more detailed picture, similar to using more classes in a histogram.

visuals.title: Ordered Stem‑and‑Leaf Plot for Text Messages

confusionCorner.body: If data are, say, 100, 105, 110, the leaf is always the last digit. For numbers like 100, the leaf is 0, not 00. If you have numbers like 1234, you might round to the nearest ten and use 123 as stem and 4 as leaf. [[imp:Always define the leaf as a single digit, and state the key clearly.]]
confusionCorner.title: Leaf Must Be One Digit!

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine you're a researcher with a list of 48 text‑message counts. You could tally them into a frequency table, but you'd lose the actual numbers. A stem‑and‑leaf plot lets you see the shape of the data while keeping every original value — like a histogram that still remembers each data point.

confusionCorner.title: Dot Plot vs. Scatter Plot
confusionCorner.body: A dot plot shows a [[imp:single]] quantitative variable along a horizontal axis. A scatter plot shows [[imp:two]] quantitative variables on horizontal and vertical axes. Don't confuse them! Dot plot = one variable; scatter plot = two.

teacherCues: Draw a horizontal axis from 70 to 160. Place a dot for each text message count as you read the data aloud.
Ask: 'Which value occurs most often? Can you see an outlier?'

examples.title: Example A – Creating a Dot Plot
examples.prompt: Create a dot plot for the text message data from Example 1. Use a horizontal axis from 70 to 160.
steps: Draw a number line from 70 to 160 with tick marks at appropriate intervals (e.g., every 10).
For each data point, place a dot above its value. 78 gets a dot; 105 gets a dot, and so on.
When a value repeats, stack the dots vertically.
The resulting plot shows a cluster around 110–130 and an outlier at 78.

A histogram is better for large data sets because it reduces clutter.

Show a Pareto chart of inventory shrinkage. Ask: 'Why are the bars arranged tallest to shortest?'

confusionCorner.body: Both display qualitative data, but a pie chart emphasizes [[imp:part‑to‑whole]] relationships; a Pareto chart emphasizes the [[imp:ranking]] of categories. Use a pie chart when you want to show proportions of a whole; use a Pareto chart when you need to highlight the most significant categories.
confusionCorner.title: Pie Chart vs. Pareto Chart

explanation: A [[kw:pie chart]] is a circle divided into sectors, where each sector's area (or central angle) is proportional to the category's relative frequency.
To find the central angle for a category: multiply 360° by the category's relative frequency.
A [[kw:Pareto chart]] is a vertical bar graph where bars are arranged in [[imp:decreasing order]] of frequency (or relative frequency), with the tallest bar on the left.
Pareto charts help highlight the most important categories; they are widely used in business for quality control and problem identification.

discoveryHook.scenario: Qualitative data — like degree types or causes of inventory loss — don't have a natural order, but we still need to see which category dominates. A pie chart shows each category as a slice of the whole. A Pareto chart orders the categories from most to least frequent, making it instantly clear where to focus.

blocks.title: Pie Charts and Pareto Charts

steps: Relative frequency: $ 455 / 1941 \approx 0.234 $ (23.4%).
Central angle: $ 360° \times 0.234 \approx 84° $ (round to nearest degree).
Draw a circle and use a protractor to mark an 84° sector. Label 'Associate's 23%'.
Repeat for all categories. The completed chart shows bachelor's as the largest slice.

steps: A Pareto chart orders bars from highest to lowest, making the biggest problems stand out.
The retailer can see immediately that employee theft and shoplifting cause the most loss.
A pie chart shows the same proportions, but the ranking isn't as visually striking.
Thus, a Pareto chart directly guides where to focus resources.

discoveryHook.scenario: Two variables can be linked: petal length and width of irises; hours worked and hourly wages; years and the number of cell phone subscribers. A scatter plot reveals whether one tends to increase with the other. A time series chart tracks a single variable over time, exposing trends and seasonal patterns.

confusionCorner.title: Scatter Plot ≠ Time Series
confusionCorner.body: Both use points, but a scatter plot has two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals (like height and weight). A time series always has [[imp:time]] as the horizontal axis and shows one variable changing over time. Don't connect dots in a scatter plot unless there's a meaningful order (which there usually isn't).

teacherCues: Plot two variables — hours worked (x) and hourly wage (y) — as points. Ask: 'What relationship do you see?'
Show a time series of cell phone subscribers over time. Ask: 'What's the overall trend?'

explanation: A [[kw:scatter plot]] graphs ordered pairs $ (x, y) $ from two quantitative variables on a coordinate plane. It shows the [[imp:relationship]] (if any) between them.
If both variables tend to increase together, the scatter plot shows a positive association; if one increases while the other decreases, it's a negative association.
A [[kw:time series]] is a data set collected at regular time intervals (e.g., daily, yearly).
A [[kw:time series chart]] plots the time variable on the horizontal axis and the quantitative variable on the vertical axis, connecting consecutive points with line segments to reveal trends.

discoveryHook.scenario: Facing a new data set, it's easy to be overwhelmed by the many graph choices. The blueprint simplifies it: first understand your data type and what you want to show, then solve by matching the data to the right graphical tool, and finally conclude by interpreting the graph's story.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Data} \;\begin{cases} \text{Qualitative} \;\begin{cases} \text{Proportions} \;\rightarrow \; \text{Pie chart} \\ \text{Ranking} \;\rightarrow \; \text{Pareto chart} \end{cases} \\ \text{Quantitative (1 var)} \;\begin{cases} \text{Small n} \;\rightarrow \; \text{Stem‑and‑leaf or dot plot} \\ \text{Large n} \;\rightarrow \; \text{Histogram} \\ \text{Over time} \;\rightarrow \; \text{Time series} \end{cases} \\ \text{Quantitative (2 vars)} \;\rightarrow \; \text{Scatter plot} \end{cases}$$

legend.meaning: Match the graph to the data and the question.

formulaCard.title: Blueprint Decision Flow

explanation: Use the Understand → Solve → Conclude blueprint for selecting and constructing a graph.
1. [[kw:Understand]]: Is the data quantitative or qualitative? How many variables? What do you want to reveal — the distribution, a comparison, a trend over time, or a relationship?

2. [[kw:Solve]]: Choose the appropriate graph. For quantitative data, consider stem‑and‑leaf plot, dot plot, histogram, frequency polygon, ogive, scatter plot, or time series chart. For qualitative data, consider pie chart or Pareto chart.
3. [[kw:Conclude]]: Draw the graph accurately, label axes, provide a title, and describe the key findings in plain language.

examples.title: Example A – Selecting a Graph
examples.prompt: You have the number of complaints received by the BBB for five different types of businesses. Which graph best shows which type has the most complaints?
steps: Understand: Qualitative data (business types), goal = rank by frequency.
Solve: A [[kw:Pareto chart]] arranges bars from highest to lowest frequency, making the ranking obvious.
Conclude: Use a Pareto chart; auto dealers will be the tallest bar if they have the most complaints.

examples.prompt: You have the exam scores of 25 students. Explain to a partner why a stem‑and‑leaf plot might be preferable to a histogram.
steps: A stem‑and‑leaf plot retains all original data values, so you can find the exact scores, not just ranges.
For a small class, you can see the distribution and identify individual performances.
A histogram would group scores into intervals, losing exact values.
examples.title: Example B – Justifying a Stem‑and‑Leaf Plot

examples.prompt: You have annual GDP and annual manufacturing employment for 20 years. You want to see if they're related. Which graph?
steps: Understand: Two quantitative variables (GDP and employment), want to see relationship.
Solve: A [[kw:scatter plot]] displays the relationship between two variables.
Conclude: Plot GDP on x‑axis, employment on y‑axis. If you want to see trends over time, you could also make a time series chart for each variable separately.
